title: Decision Boundary
excerpt: A decision boundary is the point in an automated or AI-assisted workflow where human judgment must be actively exercised. It is functional only when the interaction design supports informed, deliberate judgment rather than passive acceptance.
metaDescription: Definition of a decision boundary in automated and AI-assisted workflows, including placement, friction, information, and evidence limits.
summary: A decision boundary separates system action, system recommendation, and human judgment. In this documentation, the term refers to an interaction design choice that determines whether human oversight is functional or only nominal.

bodyMarkdown:
## Definition

A decision boundary is the point in an automated or AI-assisted workflow where human judgment must be actively exercised rather than passively supplied through acceptance of a system recommendation.

At a decision boundary, the system is designed to require a genuine human decision. The interaction does not merely allow override as a theoretical option. It structures the workflow so that consequential acceptance cannot occur without deliberate human engagement.

Decision boundaries are design choices. Boundary placement, boundary friction, and information provision all affect whether human judgment is exercised in practice or exists only in principle.

## Meaning in Creative Navy's documentation

In Creative Navy's documentation, a decision boundary is treated as an interaction-level mechanism for making human oversight functional. The relevant distinction is not whether a policy says a human can intervene. The relevant distinction is whether the interface makes human judgment possible, informed, and necessary at the point where consequence enters the workflow.

Decision boundaries apply to AI-enabled products, automated workflows, and systems where an interface could present an action as available even when the system cannot evidence that availability. The term is therefore broader than AI recommendation design, although it is especially important in AI-assisted contexts.

## Nominal and functional decision boundaries differ at the interface

A nominal decision boundary exists in policy or architecture but does not actively support human judgment. A user may technically be able to intervene, but the interface may not provide the information needed for informed approval. The cognitive cost of approval may be lower than the cognitive cost of evaluation. The default workflow may carry the user through the boundary without prompting genuine deliberation.

A functional decision boundary actively supports and requires human judgment. The relevant information is present at the decision point. Acceptance friction is calibrated to the consequence of the decision. Passive acceptance of an AI recommendation is not the path of least resistance.

The difference between a nominal decision boundary and a functional decision boundary is the interface, not the policy.

## What a functional decision boundary includes

A functional decision boundary has three design components: boundary placement, boundary friction calibration, and information provision at the boundary.

### Boundary placement identifies where human judgment is required

Boundary placement determines where a workflow requires active human judgment. Placement is informed by consequence level, AI confidence reliability, and governance requirements.

Higher consequence decisions require more active human judgment. Decision boundaries are also important where AI confidence is variable or where the AI operates near the edge of its reliable zone. Some domains require human judgment at specific decision points regardless of AI reliability.

### Boundary friction calibration makes acceptance proportional to consequence

Boundary friction calibration sets the interaction cost of acceptance in relation to the consequence of acceptance. High-consequence decisions need confirmation steps that require the user to actively engage with what they are accepting. Low-consequence reversible decisions can use minimal friction.

Uniform friction across all decisions is not the design standard described here. Calibration must be specific to consequence.

### Information provision makes the decision evaluable at the boundary

Information provision at the boundary means the user has the information required to make an informed decision at the moment of decision. A boundary that requires approval of something the user cannot evaluate is only nominal.

Relevant context can include AI confidence, supporting evidence, historical performance, and consequence of approval. The required context depends on the decision and the system.

## Decision boundaries in AI-enabled products

In AI-enabled products, decision boundaries define the partition between autonomous AI decision-making, AI recommendation with human confirmation, and human judgment independent of the AI recommendation.

This three-way partition is a design decision. Where each boundary sits determines whether human oversight is real or nominal. The boundaries must be placed before the interaction design is built around them. The interaction design enforces the boundary, but the boundary is a prior conceptual decision.

## Override design enforces the decision boundary

Override design is the enforcement mechanism at a decision boundary. An override that is technically available but cognitively expensive to execute is not a functional boundary.

Override parity is the design standard for boundaries where genuine independent judgment is required. Override parity means that overriding an AI recommendation should require no more cognitive effort than accepting it.

## Examples in practice

In the Puraite AI systematic review case, the decision boundary was placed at each inclusion or exclusion screening decision. Blinded mode kept the AI recommendation unavailable until after human assessment was recorded. Override parity removed the friction asymmetry that was making acceptance the path of least resistance. The boundary was made functional through information sequencing and friction calibration.

In the Callsign fraud detection case, the separation between evaluation mode and configuration mode functioned as decision boundary design. The boundary sat between reviewing how a policy behaves and making changes to live fraud strategy. Modification was structurally impossible during evaluation, so the boundary was enforced architecturally rather than through friction alone.

In the Kardion MCS Controller case, the two-step rotary knob confirmation for flow rate adjustment was decision boundary design at the device-interaction level. The boundary sat between adjusting the knob and executing the flow adjustment. The second deliberate confirmation step calibrated friction to the clinical consequence of unintended adjustment. The evidence for this example is formative evaluation only.

In the Schone Airspace Group ground control station interface for connected aircraft, the system has no model, performs no inference, and makes no recommendations. The decision boundaries are drawn against a radio link, a protocol, and a clock. This extends the term beyond AI framing: boundary discipline applies wherever a system could act, or appear ready to act, on state it cannot evidence.

In the Schone Airspace Group case, an uncertain aircraft state blocks an optimistic command display. Where link condition and sample freshness cannot establish eligibility, the action shows availability as unknown rather than ready. The accepted cost was the sacrifice of apparent immediate availability in uncertain conditions in order to preserve the accuracy of command affordances. The boundary is enforced before the decision point because the operator is not offered a decision the system cannot support.

In the Schone Airspace Group case, interface target selection does not confer flight-controller authority. Eligibility and command-channel permission are independent checks resolved outside the interface. The accepted cost was an extra status label in exchange for not using one selected icon to represent several unrelated system permissions. Selection and authority are kept on opposite sides of the boundary by design.

## Evidence basis

The definition is conceptual and is supported by documented examples from Puraite, Callsign, Kardion, and Schone Airspace Group. The examples show different enforcement mechanisms: information sequencing, friction calibration, read-only architectural separation, deliberate confirmation, and explicit state eligibility.

The Puraite, Callsign, and Kardion examples sit inside AI-enabled or automated decision-support contexts. The Schone Airspace Group example is not an AI system. Its unknowns are properties of a link and a protocol, not of a probability distribution.

## Boundaries and limits

A decision boundary does not prove that the human will make the correct decision. It defines where the interface requires and supports human judgment.

The Schone Airspace Group design decisions describe what was designed, not a measured result. The product is built and in test, not deployed. The available evidence does not establish that the design prevents accidents, wrong-aircraft commands, or operator error.

The Kardion MCS Controller example is limited to formative evaluation. It should not be treated as evidence of a summative or deployed outcome.

## Related pages

Decision boundary is closely related to human oversight, decision quality, cognitive load, state visibility, operational clarity, transition clarity, high-consequence decisions, and trust calibration. The documented examples also connect the term to Puraite, Callsign, Kardion, and Schone Airspace Group.
